issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings in a criminal appeal are not disturbed absent a serious infirmity in the assessment of evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court accepted the prosecution account of the occurrence and the evidence of the eyewitnesses.
The Supreme Court found no cogent ground or serious infirmity in the concurrent assessment of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent factual findings were accepted and left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: On appeal, concurrent findings supported by an assessment of the evidence and free from serious infirmity are not open to reassessment merely because the opposing version is urged. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same factual findings after assessing the evidence.
predicates.no_serious_evidentiary_infirmity: The reviewing court found no serious flaw in the lower courts’ assessment of the evidence.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges matching factual findings and the evidence assessment has no serious infirmity, those findings are left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of private defence does not justify chasing and assaulting a party that is fleeing after the immediate threat has ceased.
material_facts: The lower courts found that the prosecution party was unarmed and was not the aggressor.
The accused chased members of that party as they fled and assaulted them at a considerable distance.
The Supreme Court accepted those concurrent findings and found no basis for a right of private defence.
issues.conclusion: The claim of private defence, including the alternative claim that the accused exceeded such a right, was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment applies the principle that any right of private defence available at the outset ceases when the threat has passed; pursuing and assaulting fleeing persons cannot then be justified as defence. The Court considered the defence under the Indian Penal Code but cited no earlier case.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.accused_party_found_to_be_aggressor: The courts found that the accused party initiated the aggression and that the opposing party was not the aggressor.
predicates.opposing_party_fled: Members of the opposing party ran away from the accused party.
predicates.accused_pursued_and_assaulted_fleeing_pa: The accused party chased and assaulted members of the opposing party after they had fled.

issues.definition: If an accused party found to be the aggressor pursues and assaults a fleeing opposing party in a criminal appeal, the private-defence claim is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A shared intention to kill may be inferred where identified assailants jointly attack a victim with deadly weapons on vital parts and cause death.
material_facts: The eyewitness evidence accepted by both lower courts identified three assailants as striking the deceased with spears on vital parts of the body.
The deceased died from the assault, and the Supreme Court found the evidence sufficient even without relying on one challenged witness.
The Supreme Court found no adequate basis to displace the lower courts’ conclusion about the assailants’ intention.
issues.conclusion: The murder convictions of the three assailants on the basis of common intention were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, inferring common intention to kill from the assailants’ coordinated use of deadly weapons against vital parts of the victim and the resulting death. No earlier case was relied on.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accepted_evidence_identifies_joint_assailants and deadly_weapons_used_on_vital_parts and victim_died_from_assault

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging convictions.

predicates.deadly_weapons_used_on_vital_parts: The assailants used deadly weapons to strike vital parts of the victim’s body.
predicates.victim_died_from_assault: The victim died as a result of the assault.

issues.definition: When accepted evidence identifies joint assailants who use deadly weapons on vital parts and cause the victim’s death, the joint murder conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly sharing an object to assault may be held liable for grievous hurt likely to be caused by the armed attack and for the associated rioting and assault proved against them.
material_facts: The courts found that the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the opposing party.
The armed group chased and assaulted members of that party, who were fleeing, and the evidence established grievous and other injuries.
The Supreme Court found the likelihood of grievous hurt and the evidence supporting the assault convictions sufficiently established.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for rioting, grievous hurt with group liability, and the separately proved assaults were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 147 and 148 of the Indian Penal Code to rioting, and Sections 326/149 and 323 to grievous hurt and other assault. It held that where an armed unlawful assembly shares an object to assault, the likelihood of grievous hurt from the attack supports group liability for that offence. No earlier case was relied on.

predicates.assault_causes_or_is_likely_to_cause_gri: The attack caused grievous hurt or, in the circumstances found, grievous hurt was likely to result.

issues.definition: When an armed unlawful assembly shares an object to assault and its attack causes or is likely to cause grievous hurt, the group assault and rioting convictions are upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to recover a victim’s body does not by itself prevent a finding of death or concealment when accepted evidence establishes the fatal assault and removal of the body.
material_facts: Accepted eyewitness evidence established that the deceased was fatally assaulted and that members of the accused party wrapped and carried away the body toward a river.
The body was not recovered despite a search, so no post-mortem examination took place.
The Supreme Court accepted the lower courts’ findings about the death and removal of the body.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a recovered body did not undermine the findings of death or the convictions for removing or concealing the body.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 201 of the Indian Penal Code to the proved removal and disappearance of the body and rejected the contention that non-recovery of the body prevented proof of death. No earlier case was relied on.

predicates.accepted_evidence_establishes_body_remov: Evidence accepted by the courts establishes that persons removed or concealed the victim’s body.
predicates.body_not_recovered: The victim’s body was not recovered.

issues.definition: When accepted evidence establishes a fatal assault and removal of the body, non-recovery of the body does not prevent the death and disappearance findings from being sustained.

issues.legal_issue: Delay or failure to hold a test identification parade does not establish prejudice when the identifying witnesses already knew the accused and the parade evidence is not relied upon.
material_facts: The accused sought prompt test identification parades, but the identifying witnesses apparently knew them.
The Court considered that a parade would have little value in the circumstances and did not rely on parade evidence.
One proposed identifying witness died before giving evidence, and the Supreme Court found no prejudice from the delay.
issues.conclusion: The objection based on the delay or absence of test identification parades was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A test identification parade is corroborative rather than substantive evidence. In the circumstances found here, where the identifying witnesses apparently knew the accused and the parade evidence was not relied upon, delay in holding a parade did not establish prejudice. No earlier case was relied on.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.identifying_witnesses_knew_accused: The identifying witnesses apparently knew the accused before the identification process.
predicates.identification_parade_not_relied_on: The reviewing court did not rely on identification parade evidence to sustain the convictions.

issues.definition: If identifying witnesses knew the accused and the court did not rely on parade evidence, the identification objection is rejected in the criminal appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A challenged declaration about an injured witness’s own assailant does not displace accepted eyewitness evidence of another assault when the declaration is unreliable and the remaining evidence independently supports the finding.
material_facts: A declaration by an injured witness attributed that witness’s injuries to one accused but did not provide a reliable basis to displace the evidence about the fatal assault.
The trial court did not rely on the declaration, and its recorder was not examined; the declaration indicated that the witness was not fully conscious.
The High Court found sufficient evidence from other eyewitnesses even excluding the challenged witness’s testimony, and the Supreme Court agreed.
issues.conclusion: The declaration did not justify discarding the accepted eyewitness evidence or overturning the murder convictions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the declaration’s reliability in light of the circumstances in which it was recorded and the independent eyewitness evidence. It cited no earlier case or separate statutory provision for this evidentiary assessment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.challenged_declaration_has_reliability_c: The declaration was recorded in circumstances raising doubt about the declarant’s condition or the reliability of the account.
predicates.independent_accepted_evidence_supports_c: Evidence independent of the challenged declaration, accepted by the courts, supports the conviction.

issues.definition: When a challenged declaration has reliability concerns and independent accepted evidence supports the conviction, the declaration does not displace that conviction.
